fields.h1: What Are the Spiritual Gifts? And How to Find Yours
fields.meta_title: What Are the Spiritual Gifts? And How to Find Yours
fields.description: Every Christian is given at least one spiritual gift. Here is what the spiritual gifts are, what they are for, and how to discover and use the ones God gave you.
fields.body_html:
If you have ever wondered what you have to offer the church — or felt that the gifted people are always someone else — here is news worth hearing: every single Christian has been given at least one spiritual gift. The Holy Spirit does not equip only pastors and missionaries; he equips ordinary believers, and he has equipped you. The question is not whether you have a gift, but which one, and whether you are using it.

So what exactly are the spiritual gifts, what are they for, and how do you find yours? Here is a clear, biblical guide.

What a spiritual gift is

A spiritual gift is a God-given ability, granted by the Holy Spirit, to serve others and build up the church. Paul lays out the pattern: “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit … To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:4–7). Notice three things. The gifts are varied — God delights in a diversity of abilities, not a uniform crowd. They come from the Spirit — they are not merely natural talents you were born with, but abilities the Spirit gives and empowers. And they are “for the common good” — never trophies for the individual, but tools for the whole body.

Peter says the same: “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace” (1 Peter 4:10). The gifts are grace made practical — God’s kindness flowing through one believer to reach another.

The gifts named in Scripture

The Bible gives several lists — in Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12, and Ephesians 4 — and they overlap without being identical, which suggests they are illustrations rather than an exhaustive catalogue. Among them: teaching, serving, encouraging, giving generously, leading, showing mercy (Romans 12:6–8); wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, discernment (1 Corinthians 12); and the equipping roles of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, given “to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12).

Note that last phrase carefully: the “up-front” gifts exist to equip everyone else for ministry. The New Testament knows nothing of a church where a gifted few perform and the rest watch. Every member is a minister, each carrying a gift the others need.

Who decides which gift you get?

Here is a freeing truth: you do not choose your gift, and you cannot earn a “better” one. “All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). The Spirit distributes the gifts according to his wisdom and the church’s need — which means your gift is not an accident or an afterthought. It is a deliberate assignment from God, perfectly fitted to the part he means you to play. Comparison and envy have no place here; the eye does not resent the hand, because the body needs both.

R. A. Torrey, who wrote with unusual clarity on the Spirit in The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit, stressed that the gifts are not the possession of a spiritual elite but the birthright of every believer — and that the great tragedy is not a lack of gifting but a failure to use what has been given.

The one thing greater than the gifts

It would be a serious mistake to chase gifts while neglecting the thing that must accompany them. Right in the middle of his teaching on gifts, Paul stops to say: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers … but have not love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1–2). Gifts without love are worse than useless; they are noise. A church can be spectacularly gifted and spiritually bankrupt. So the goal is never gifting for its own sake, but gifts exercised in love, for the good of others — the fruit of the Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit traveling together, as God intends.

This also settles the question of motive. The measure of a gift well used is not how impressive it looks but how much it builds others up: “strive to excel in building up the church” (1 Corinthians 14:12). Even a quiet gift of mercy or service, done in love, is worth more in God’s eyes than a dazzling gift used to draw attention to oneself. This is deeply freeing for anyone who has felt overlooked: the gifts that keep a church alive are mostly the unglamorous ones — the people who serve, encourage, give, and show mercy behind the scenes — and heaven notices every one of them.

Natural talent and spiritual gift

People often ask how a spiritual gift differs from a natural talent. The two can overlap — God frequently takes the abilities he already built into you and sets them on fire by his Spirit for the church’s good. But they are not the same. A natural talent can be exercised by anyone for any purpose; a spiritual gift is the Spirit’s enabling, given to a believer, aimed at building up the body of Christ and empowered by God rather than by mere ability. A gifted musician may play beautifully by talent, but the gift becomes spiritual when the Spirit uses that playing to lift hearts to God. The same skill, surrendered to Christ and empowered by his Spirit for others, becomes something more than it was. So do not despise the ordinary abilities God has given you — offer them to him, and watch what he does with them.

A word on the more debated gifts

Sincere Christians differ over whether some of the more dramatic gifts — miracles, healing, tongues, prophecy — operate today as they did in the early church, and godly people land in different places. This article does not try to settle that long debate. But two things unite believers across it. First, no one should despise or forbid what God is genuinely doing: “Do not quench the Spirit.” Second, no gift, however striking, is proof of spiritual maturity — Corinth was a gifted church and a deeply immature one. Whatever you conclude about the spectacular gifts, do not let the debate distract you from the plain command that unites us all: find the gift God has given you, and use it in love to serve his people. The church is not weakened by a shortage of gifts. It is weakened by gifts left unused, and strengthened every time one more believer finds theirs and begins, however humbly, to give it away.

How to discover and use your gift

If the Spirit has given you a gift, how do you find it and put it to work? A few practical steps:

  • Start serving. Gifts are usually discovered in action, not in a quiet room. Say yes to needs in your church — teach, help, give, visit, pray — and watch where God seems to bear fruit through you.
  • Notice where you are effective and glad. Your gift often sits where genuine effectiveness meets genuine joy — the service that builds others up and that you feel most alive doing.
  • Ask others. The body sees what you cannot. Trusted believers can often name the gift operating in you before you can name it yourself.
  • Desire the gifts that build up. Paul says, “earnestly desire the higher gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31) — not the flashiest, but those that most serve others. It is right to ask God for gifts that will bless his people.
  • Use it in love, and steward it. A gift is a trust, not a possession (1 Peter 4:10). Develop it, practice it, and give it away freely for the good of the church.

Catherine Booth, preaching on The Holy Ghost, pressed the church to stop leaving the Spirit’s power unclaimed. The same applies to his gifts. God has not left you empty-handed. Somewhere in you is an ability the Spirit gave, that your church needs, and that will only come alive as you offer it. You were not saved to sit on the sidelines — you were gifted for a part only you can play. Find it, and give it away.

And do not wait until you feel qualified. Most Christians discover and develop their gifts by stepping out before they feel ready, and finding the Spirit meeting them in the act of serving. The gift grows in the using, like a muscle; it withers in the hiding. A church full of members who have each found and are faithfully exercising their gift is an unstoppable thing — not because any one person is impressive, but because the whole body is working “as each part is working properly” (Ephesians 4:16). That is the picture the New Testament holds out: not a stage with a few stars, but a body in which every member matters and every gift is needed — including yours.
